<reason>Both sides argued at a high level with clean structure and no fake sourcing. CON's strongest lines — that legitimacy does not detect error, that the peaceful-removal mechanism is parasitic on competent institutions and information, and that the governed are harmed by content rather than pedigree — created real pressure, and CON honestly answered the mill-town question rather than dodging. But CON's case repeatedly conceded the ordering PRO needed: in answer to A1, CON granted that the public may revoke the mandate and that no body overrules the legislature, then retreated to "revocation is usually a mistake," which PRO correctly characterized as advice rather than entitlement. PRO also blunted CON's central lever by clarifying early ([A2.6], reaffirmed [A4.5]) that it never claimed voters detect error, so CON's repeated reliance on "voters aren't smarter" as a fatal concession did less work than CON's closing asserted. PRO's delegation argument (mandates chartered, objective functions set, revocable) absorbed CON's best institutional evidence — central banks, courts, drug approval — and reframed it as demonstrating rather than refuting the case, and CON's "proves too much / confession" reply never named an alternative source of authority. Progression favored PRO: it narrowed the clash to "competence is measured against a target it cannot select," which CON only partly answered by shrinking the moral residue to a rare case. CON's closing landed the best counter-frame ("authority without competence still hurts people; it just hurts them lawfully"), but by then it depended on a metric shift PRO had already pre-empted with "outcomes win begs which outcomes." CON also incurred a small execution cost with a clipped Rebuttal 2 that lost its weighing punchline.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's turn on Flint: CON offered poisoned water as the paradigm of technocratic necessity, and PRO showed the switch was made by a state-appointed emergency manager installed over an elected council to hit a cost target, with residents ignored for months. CON's reply (voice was present but useless; an engineer found the lead) partly held, but PRO's follow-up — voice supplied the reason to look, and accountability dismantled the insulated regime — left CON's own flagship example reading as insulated competence causing the harm.</best_rebuttal>
